item.content:encoded:
I admit I've done a poor job of explaining myself. I mean for there to be a distinction between physical impossibility and logical impossibility. I agree that his traveling backwards in time is probably inconsistent with the laws of our universe. (I believe it's been shown that it's at least physically possible that wormholes could be used as time machines to the past, but they could only travel back as far as the opening of the wormhole. At any rate, this doesn't apply here.) This would mean that traveling back in time is physically impossible, but in the spirit of the site I'm perfectly willing to accept that an SCP can do the physically impossible.

What I don't think can be done is the logically impossible. If SCP-196 died in 200X before he could travel back to 196X, then it would be the case that he both made it back to 196X and didn't make it back to 196X, which is an instance of 'P and not P'—a logical impossibility. I think this is more or less understood, and that's why some say a paradox would arise if SCP-196 died in 200X. I would say, though, that the laws of logic (which apply in every universe, not just ours) forbid an actual paradox to take place, so SCP-196 cannot die in 200X; that is, no matter what happens, SCP-196 will not die before he makes it back to 196X. The deconstruction of these sorts of time-travel "paradoxes" is more or less complete in the contemporary literature of metaphysics, philosophy of physics, and even physics itself.

If there's still a disagreement, then what we disagree upon is whether SCP-196 can break the laws of logic. Again, I agree that he can break the laws of physics to be able to time travel in this manner, but I don't think he's anywhere near the caliber to be able to break the laws of logic. [On a loosely related note: I'm tempted to think that no SCP can break the laws of logic. For example, I'd say SCP-682 (and other ultimately eldritch beings that do whatever ridiculous things), who appears to be both alive and dead simultaneously, isn't breaking the laws of logic; it simply calls into question whether we (the real "us" and the Foundation) have the correct understanding of what it means to be alive. Even the SCPs that appear to be doing the logically impossible must not be, because they aren't bringing about paradoxes that cancel the universe.]

item.content:encoded:
I would like to advocate Euclid classification.

It's either the case that time is one-dimensional or that time is multi-dimensional. If time is one-dimensional, then SCP-196 cannot die before he returns to 196X, because the past cannot be changed. If time is multi-dimensional, then the SCP-196 in captivity can die, because the SCP-196 that died in 196X is not the very same SCP-196 in captivity (they are from alternate timelines). While they may hardly know the actual nature of time (whether it is one- or multi-dimensional), Foundation scientists—with regularly above-average cleverness—must recognize that it is one or the other, and since a paradox cannot arise in either case, they would conclude that there is no reason to designate SCP-196 as Keter. In fact, there is nothing intrinsically anomalous about SCP-196 (unless he can time-travel of his own will); nevertheless, I can imagine the Foundation's wanting to retain SCP-196 because he is a known time-traveler: the Foundation may hope to bear witness to SCP-196's actual time-traveling and to learn more about their possibly harnessing such technology or abilities. So, they would designate SCP-196 as Euclid to uphold a standard of security.
